tool.name: PRISMClimateData

summary.para:
View online help files: https://www.jennessent.com/data-tools/prism-climate-data.html
Gets PRISM climate grids for a study area and writes them to one netCDF file with a time dimension: precipitation, temperature, dew point, vapor pressure deficit and solar radiation, by day, month or year, for any span of dates. PRISM, of the PRISM Group at Oregon State University, maps the climate of the conterminous United States on grids of about 4 km and about 800 m, by month and year since 1895 and by day since 1981. PRISM's web service sends one whole-country grid for each variable and date; this tool fetches each grid once, keeps it, and cuts it to the study area. The tool is meant to download PRISM data and to assemble it into one file that is ready for analysis. A second tool, still in the planning stages, will calculate PRISM statistics for the points, lines and polygons that intersect that file. No account is needed. Conterminous United States only. Works at every license level.

tool.usage:
What the tool writes. One netCDF file that holds every variable and date you chose, cut to the study area. Each climate variable is a variable of the file, and the dates are its time dimension, so the file is a true multidimensional dataset: ArcGIS Pro shows it with a list of variables and a date for each time step, and R and Python read it as they read any climate file. The cells are PRISM's own cells with PRISM's own values. Nothing is resampled or reprojected.
How PRISM delivers its data, and why the tool keeps files. PRISM's web service sends one grid for each request: one variable on one date, always for the whole conterminous United States, whatever the size of the study area. Forty years of monthly precipitation and mean temperature are 960 requests. A 4 km grid is a file of about 2 MB and an 800 m grid is a file of 15 to 60 MB (measured in November 2026). The tool waits 2 seconds between requests, as PRISM's own sample script does, and tells you before it starts how many grids it will fetch, about how large they are, and how long the waiting alone will take. It keeps every file it downloads in a folder, so a later run for more dates, more variables or another study area fetches only what is not there yet. PRISM's rule on downloads, in its own words: "if a file is downloaded twice in a 24-hour period, no more downloads of that file will be allowed during that period. Repeated excessive download activity may result in IP address blocking."
The folder of downloaded files is remembered. PRISM's files are whole-country grids, as useful to the next project as to this one, so the folder that keeps them should not belong to any one project. Choose a folder on a drive with room: forty years of monthly grids of one variable are about 1 GB at 4 km and tens of gigabytes at 800 m. The tool saves the folder you run with for your Windows user account, outside the project, so the next time the tool is opened, in this project or any other, the folder is already filled in and the grids in it are found. Choose a different folder and that one is remembered from then on; the files in the old one are not moved. Before any folder has been chosen the files go to a folder named PRISM_downloads in your Windows user folder, such as C:\Users\maria\PRISM_downloads. The setting is kept in the file prism_settings.json in %LOCALAPPDATA%\JennessEnterprises\WildlifeTools; deleting that file makes the tool forget the folder.
The variables. Precipitation is rain and melted snow, in millimeters. The temperatures and the dew point are in degrees Celsius; PRISM calculates the mean temperature as the average of the maximum and the minimum. Vapor pressure deficit is in hectopascals. Solar radiation is the total shortwave energy received in a day, in megajoules per square meter per day, on a horizontal surface (soltotal) or on the ground as it slopes (solslope). A monthly grid of precipitation is the month's total; a monthly grid of any other variable is the average of its daily values.
Time steps. Monthly and annual grids begin in January 1895, and daily grids on 1 January 1981. A PRISM day runs from 1200 UTC to 1200 UTC and is named for the day it ends on. PRISM makes a grid when its day, month or year is over, so dates that are not over yet are left out and the tool says so. In the file each time step carries the date of its first day, and a second variable, time_bnds, holds each step's first day and the day after its last.
Annual grids are not the months added up. PRISM makes a year's precipitation grid by adding up that year's twelve monthly grids as they stood at the time, and it may reissue a monthly grid after that. The grids of 2019, fetched on 21 November 2026, show the result: near Flagstaff, Arizona, the annual precipitation grid differed from the sum of the twelve monthly grids by as much as 16 mm, and eight of those twelve monthly grids were made later than the ones the annual grid lists as its sources. Where annual and monthly values must agree, fetch the monthly grids and add or average them.
Resolution. PRISM's cells are squares of latitude and longitude on NAD 83: 2.5 arc-minutes on a side (about 4 km) or 30 arc-seconds (about 800 m). Twenty-five 800 m cells fill one 4 km cell exactly. PRISM does its modeling at 30 arc-seconds and makes each 4 km grid from the 800 m grid with a Gaussian filter, as the information file inside each 4 km grid says. A 4 km value is therefore a smoothed value, and not the plain average of the 25 cells of 800 m under it. Because the cells are squares of latitude and longitude, they narrow northward: a cell at 49 degrees north has about three quarters of the area of a cell at 30 degrees north.
Grids less than six months old. PRISM reissues a grid several times in its first six months, as more station reports arrive (eight times for a daily grid and seven for a monthly one), and calls it stable after that. The tool marks every time step whose grid was less than six months old when it was fetched, in a variable of the file named provisional, and says how many there are. When a kept file was fetched inside those six months, a later run asks PRISM whether the grid has been reissued and fetches it again if it has.
The two datasets. All networks (AN) uses every station network PRISM has, for the best estimate on each date. Long-term networks (LT) uses only the networks that have stations with 20 or more years of data, to be more consistent over time; PRISM offers it as monthly grids at 800 m, without solar radiation. In some irrigated farming areas of the West the two differ noticeably in dew point and vapor pressure deficit from the 1980s on, because AN includes stations sited in irrigated fields and LT does not.
A caution about change over time. PRISM's terms of use say: "It is not recommended that PRISM data be used to calculate very long-term trends." Each grid is made from the weather stations that reported at the time, and the stations change: they open, close and move, their instruments and their hours of observation change, and whole networks join the record. From 2002 the precipitation grids of the central and eastern United States also draw on radar. A change in a cell's values over decades can therefore come from a change in the measurements and not from a change in the climate. The LT dataset reduces this and does not remove it: PRISM asks for the same care with it. PRISM's advice is that a trend over decades be calculated carefully and, ideally, backed up with observed data.
Made for the analysis that follows. The tool is meant to download PRISM data and to assemble it into one file that is ready for analysis. A second tool, still in the planning stages, will calculate PRISM statistics for the points, lines and polygons that intersect that file. The file is laid out so that climate can be summarized for points, lines and polygons without further preparation. The study area is given at least one extra cell on every side. Every cell's center and edges are in the file (lat and lon, lat_bnds and lon_bnds), so an analysis can tell which cells lie in a polygon. Every cell's true area on the ellipsoid is in the file too (cell_area, in square kilometers), so cells can be weighted by their size. The values are stored in blocks of dates and of cells, so a map of one date and the whole series of one cell are both quick to read.
Seeing the file in a map. When the tool finishes it adds a multidimensional raster layer of each variable to the map. A layer shows one time step at a time. To step through the dates, click the layer in the Contents pane and use the Multidimensional tab: the StdTime list, or the step and play buttons. The map's time slider moves the layers too, when it holds a single date: it then steps from one date of the file to the next. ArcGIS Pro opens the time slider with a span one time step long that ends on the file's first date, and it draws a layer only when the span starts exactly on one of the file's dates (seen in ArcGIS Pro 3.7). Left that way the map is empty at first, and stepping through monthly data shows only some of the months, because the span keeps its length in days and the months do not. This add-in therefore closes the span to a single date when layers of a file this tool wrote are added to a map, whether the tool adds them or you do. It does so only when no other layer of the map uses time, so that it never hides other data, and it leaves alone a time slider that already holds a single date. Where it has not done so, close the span yourself: on the Time tab, in the Current Time group, set Span to 0. ArcGIS Pro keeps the setting with the map. When Months leaves months out, the dates are no longer evenly spaced and the time slider, which moves by one fixed step, will not land on them: use the Multidimensional tab. To add the file to another map yourself: on the Map tab, click the arrow under Add Data (the choice is in that menu, not on the button itself) and choose Multidimensional Data. In the Add Multidimensional Data window that opens, click the folder button and pick the file, check the variables to show in the Select Variables table, and click OK. No extension is needed to open, show or subset the file.
The colors of a layer. Left to itself, ArcGIS Pro takes the colors of a layer of a netCDF file from the first time step alone, and the other dates are drawn with them (tested in ArcGIS Pro 3.7). The tool therefore writes a small statistics file beside the netCDF file, with .aux.xml added to its name, that holds each variable's least and greatest value over all the time steps, and ArcGIS Pro stretches the colors of every layer of the file over those. A color then means the same value on every date, so one date can be compared with another, and a dry month shows little contrast in precipitation. To see the pattern within one date, set the layer's stretch statistics to DRA in the Symbology pane. Keep the statistics file with the netCDF file when the file is moved or copied.
The notes that go with the data. The tool writes its notes into the metadata: what a value of each variable is, the dates, the grids less than six months old, how to cite PRISM and the caution about change over time. To read them, right-click a layer of the file in the Contents pane and choose View Metadata. The metadata is kept in a small file beside the netCDF file, with .xml added to its name, and this add-in gives it to each layer of the file that arrives in a map; keep that file with the netCDF file when the file is moved or copied. The notes are inside the netCDF file too, and a layer's properties show the note of its variable: on the Source tab, under Multidimensional Info, in the row named Description. In a file of annual grids that note begins with the caution that a year's grid does not always equal its twelve monthly grids added up or averaged.
Citing PRISM. PRISM's terms of use ask that any description of the data's use state PRISM's name, its web address and the date of access, for example: PRISM Group, Oregon State University, https://prism.oregonstate.edu, accessed 16 Dec 2025. The tool writes that line, with the day of the run, into the file, into its metadata and into its messages.
Conterminous United States only. PRISM's web service covers the conterminous United States, the lower 48 states. A study area that reaches past PRISM's grid is cut at its edge, and cells over the ocean and beyond the border are no-data.

param.name: study_area
param.displayname: Study area features (points, lines or polygons; selection honored)

dialogReference.para: A layer or feature class of points, lines or polygons, in any coordinate system. Selected features are used when there is a selection, and a definition query is honored. The file covers the rectangle around the features, plus the cells added by Cells to add around the study area. Give a study area layer or a rectangle, not both.

param.name: extent
param.displayname: Or a rectangle as the study area

dialogReference.para: A rectangle, in any coordinate system. The file covers every PRISM cell the rectangle touches, plus the cells added by Cells to add around the study area. Give a study area layer or a rectangle, not both.
The variables to get. Each one becomes a variable of the netCDF file, under PRISM's short name for it (in parentheses). Each one also multiplies the number of grids to download.

bulletList.bullet_item: Precipitation (ppt) (a default): rain and melted snow, in millimeters. A month's or a year's grid is the total.
Mean temperature (tmean) (a default): degrees Celsius. PRISM calculates it as the average of the maximum and the minimum.
Mean dew point temperature (tdmean): degrees Celsius.
Solar radiation on a horizontal surface (soltotal): megajoules per square meter per day.
Solar radiation on the sloping ground (solslope): megajoules per square meter per day, on the ground as it slopes.

dialogReference.para: For every variable but precipitation, a month's grid is the average of the daily values. The two solar variables are not in the Long-term networks (LT) dataset.
Whether each time step of the file is a month, a day or a year.

bulletList.bullet_item: Monthly (the default): one grid for each month, from January 1895. Set First year and Last year, and Months to keep only some months of each year.
Daily: one grid for each day, from 1 January 1981 through yesterday. Set First day and Last day. A PRISM day runs from 1200 UTC to 1200 UTC and is named for the day it ends on.
Annual: one grid for each year, from 1895 through last year. Set First year and Last year. A year's grid need not equal its twelve monthly grids added up; see the usage notes.

dialogReference.para: The first year to get, 1895 or later. Used when Time step is Monthly or Annual, and needed then. Not used when it is Daily.

The last year to get. Used when Time step is Monthly or Annual, and needed then. Not used when it is Daily. Months and years that are not over yet have no grid: they are left out, and the tool says so.
The first day to get, 1 January 1981 or later. Used only when Time step is Daily, and needed then.
The last day to get. Used only when Time step is Daily, and needed then. PRISM's daily data end yesterday: later days are left out, and the tool says so.

The months of the year to keep, as numbers 1 (January) to 12 (December), in every year: 6, 7 and 8 keep June through August. Empty for all months. Used when Time step is Monthly or Daily. Not used when it is Annual.
The size of PRISM's cells, which are squares of latitude and longitude.

bulletList.bullet_item: 4 km (the default): cells of 2.5 arc-minutes. Each grid is a download of about 2 MB.

800 m: cells of 30 arc-seconds, twenty-five to each 4 km cell. Each grid is a download of 15 to 60 MB, whatever the size of the study area, so a long series takes much longer and much more disk space.

dialogReference.para: Which of PRISM's two time series to get.

bulletList.bullet_item: All networks (AN) (the default): made from every station network PRISM has, for the best estimate on each date. Available for every variable, time step and resolution.

Long-term networks (LT): made only from the networks that have stations with 20 or more years of data, to be more consistent over time. PRISM offers it only with Time step set to Monthly and Resolution set to 800 m, and without the two solar variables.

dialogReference.para: PRISM asks for care in calculating change over decades from either dataset; see the usage notes.

The netCDF file to write, with a name ending in .nc, in a folder (not in a geodatabase). A file of the same name is replaced, and only when the new file is complete. The tool also writes a small statistics file beside it, with .aux.xml added to the name, from which ArcGIS Pro takes the colors of the layers: keep the two together.

param.name: download_folder
param.displayname: Folder for the downloaded PRISM files (remembered for every project)

dialogReference.para: The folder that keeps the whole-country files PRISM sends, and where the tool looks first for a grid before downloading it. Choose a folder outside any one project, on a drive with room: the files are as useful to the next project as to this one.

A folder that several people share. The folder can be on a network drive that several people use. When everyone who works with PRISM data chooses the same folder there, a file one person has downloaded is not downloaded again by another. Each person chooses the folder once, on their own computer. Several people can run the tool at the same time: a file takes its place in the folder only when its download is complete.

The tool remembers the folder. The folder you run with is saved for your Windows user account, not in the project. The next time the tool is opened, in this project or any other, the box already holds it, and a script that gives no folder uses it. Choose another folder at any time and that one is remembered from then on. The files in the old folder are not moved: move them yourself, or the grids in it will be downloaded again when they are needed. A folder is remembered only when Keep the downloaded files for later runs is checked.

Before any folder has been chosen, the files go to a folder named PRISM_downloads in your Windows user folder, such as C:\Users\maria\PRISM_downloads. If the remembered folder has been deleted, the tool makes it again in the same place. If it cannot be found at all, for example because it is on a drive that is not connected, the tool says so and uses that PRISM_downloads folder for the run.
Inside the folder the files keep PRISM's own names, in a folder for each dataset, resolution and variable, such as an_4km\ppt\prism_ppt_us_25m_202001.zip.

param.name: margin_cells
param.displayname: Cells to add around the study area

dialogReference.para: How many more cells to keep on every side of the rectangle around the study area, from 0 to 1,000. The default is 1, so that every feature of the study area has whole cells all round it, which a later summary needs for points near the edge.

param.name: keep_downloads
param.displayname: Keep the downloaded files for later runs

dialogReference.para: Checked (the default), the files this run downloads stay in the folder, and a later run reuses them. Unchecked, each file this run downloads is deleted as soon as its cells have been read.

A run never deletes a file that was in the folder before it began. Unchecking this box affects only the files this run downloads. A run that needs only grids that are already in the folder downloads nothing and deletes nothing. To delete PRISM files that an earlier run saved, use Windows File Explorer.

Keeping the files takes disk space, about 2 MB for each 4 km grid and 15 to 60 MB for each 800 m grid. Not keeping them means that a later run downloads them again, and PRISM allows a file to be downloaded only twice in 24 hours.

The tool estimates the size of what it must download before it starts, and stops without downloading anything when the estimate is larger than this many gigabytes. The default is 5. Files already in the folder do not count. Raise it for a request you mean to make; it is there so that a slip in the dates cannot start a download of hundreds of gigabytes.
The number of time steps in the file.
A multidimensional raster layer of each variable, for the map. Each layer shows one time step at a time; the usage notes say how to step through the dates.

scriptExample.title: PRISM Climate Data example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Thirty years of monthly precipitation and mean temperature for a study area, at 4 km.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your install path # variables options (several are separated by semicolons, each in single quotes): # 'Precipitation (ppt)', 'Minimum temperature (tmin)', 'Mean temperature (tmean)', # 'Maximum temperature (tmax)', 'Mean dew point temperature (tdmean)', # 'Minimum vapor pressure deficit (vpdmin)', 'Maximum vapor pressure deficit (vpdmax)', # 'Solar radiation on a horizontal surface (soltotal)', # 'Solar radiation on the sloping ground (solslope)' # time_step options: "Monthly", "Daily", "Annual" # resolution options: "4 km", "800 m" # dataset options: "All networks (AN)", "Long-term networks (LT)" # months options: 1 to 12, for example months="6;7;8" arcpy.jenness.PRISMClimateData( study_area=r"D:\data\wildlife.gdb\Study_Area", variables="'Precipitation (ppt)';'Mean temperature (tmean)'", time_step="Monthly", year_from=1991, year_to=2020, out_netcdf=r"D:\data\PRISM_monthly_1991_2020.nc")

scriptExample.title: Daily maximum temperature for the summers of five years
scriptExample.para: June through August of 2020 to 2024, by day. The folder given for the downloaded files is remembered, so later runs use it without being told, in this project or any other.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your install path arcpy.jenness.PRISMClimateData( study_area=r"D:\data\wildlife.gdb\Study_Area", variables="'Maximum temperature (tmax)'", time_step="Daily", date_from="2020-06-01", date_to="2024-08-31", months="6;7;8", out_netcdf=r"D:\data\PRISM_tmax_summers.nc", download_folder=r"D:\PRISM_downloads")

scriptExample.title: Reading the file afterward
scriptExample.para: The monthly series of one cell, and the map of one month, read with the netCDF4 package that ships with ArcGIS Pro. No extension is needed.
scriptExample.code: import netCDF4 ds = netCDF4.Dataset(r"D:\data\PRISM_monthly_1991_2020.nc") dates = netCDF4.num2date(ds["time"][:], ds["time"].units, only_use_cftime_datetimes=False) lat, lon = ds["lat"][:], ds["lon"][:] # cell centers; the rows run north to south row = abs(lat - 35.20).argmin() # the cell that holds 35.20 N, 111.65 W col = abs(lon - (-111.65)).argmin() series = ds["ppt"][:, row, col] # every month's precipitation in that cell, in mm july_2019 = ds["tmean"][[d.year == 2019 and d.month == 7 for d in dates].index(True)] area = ds["cell_area"][:] # square kilometers, for weighting cells ds.close()
